This vignette fits and internally validates conditional treatment-effect scores for count outcomes. The [companion ATE example](Count-examples.html) estimates the population-average effect using the same data. Score fitting and validation are distinct; estimated subgroups from the fitting sample are not independent validation.

## Prepare the data

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(precmed)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
data(countExample)
```

The example uses 4,000 simulated observations based on a multiple sclerosis claims-data scenario. In the packaged data, `age` is centered at approximately 46.2 years and `previous_cost` is centered at approximately 13,824 USD and divided by 20,172 USD. The outcome is the number of relapses during observed follow-up, and `years` provides exposure time. The score is interpreted on the conditional rate-ratio scale.

## Estimate CATE scores 

A CATE score describes the estimated treatment effect conditional on baseline
covariates. Here the score is a log rate ratio for drug 1 versus drug 0;
exponentiating it gives the corresponding conditional relapse rate ratio. Lower
scores indicate greater estimated benefit from drug 1.

### Specify the outcome and treatment models

The outcome formula specifies the relapse count and covariates used for the
outcome models and scores. The offset accounts for follow-up time when modelling
rates. Outcome models are fitted separately by treatment arm, so treatment is
not included in this formula. The treatment-model formula specifies treatment
on the left and baseline covariates on the right; it estimates propensity
scores, the probabilities of treatment conditional on those covariates.

Both formulas are needed because the doubly robust scores and subgroup effect
estimates combine outcome predictions with propensity scores. T-learner scores
use outcome predictions alone, but the treatment model is still used for the
subgroup estimates reported by `catefit()`. In a randomized trial, an
intercept-only treatment model can reflect a common assignment probability.

```{r}
outcome_formula <- y ~ age + female + previous_treatment + previous_cost +
  previous_number_relapses + offset(log(years))
ps_formula <- trt ~ age + previous_treatment
```

### Choose how to construct scores

`benefit_method` selects the score-construction approach; `outcome_method`
selects the outcome-model method for each score:

* A **T-learner** fits an outcome model in each treatment arm and compares
  predicted relapse rates. The available outcome methods include Poisson,
  negative binomial and boosting.
* **Two-regression** combines initial outcome predictions with propensity
  scores and fits separate augmented outcome regressions before comparing the
  two arms.
* **Contrast regression** combines initial outcome predictions with propensity
  scores to fit a model for the treatment contrast directly.

The latter two are doubly robust methods [@yadlowsky2020estimation]. Their
interpretation relies on causal identification, positivity and appropriate
model assumptions; propensity-score truncation can affect robustness. See
Chapter 17 for more on treatment effect heterogeneity and CATE prediction
[@hoogland2026introduction].

### Fit five scores

Entries in `outcome_method` and `benefit_method` are paired in order. This call
fits Poisson and boosting T-learners, two-regression and contrast-regression
scores using Poisson initial outcome models, and a negative binomial T-learner.
`higher.y = FALSE` ranks lower estimated relapse rate ratios as greater
benefit. We set `n.cores = 1` for boosting and a seed for reproducibility.
The scores and subgroup effects are fitted on the full dataset; they do not on
their own establish performance in new patients.

```{r example_catefit, eval = T, echo = T, cache = doc.cache}
fit_cate <- catefit(
  response = "count",
  data = countExample,
  outcome_model = outcome_formula,
  outcome_method = c("poisson", "boosting", "poisson", "poisson", "negative_binomial"),
  benefit_method = c("t_learner", "t_learner", "two_regression",
                     "contrast_regression", "t_learner"),
  ps_model = ps_formula,
  initial.predictor.method = "poisson",
  higher.y = FALSE, 
  seed = 999,
  n.cores = 1
)
```

## Inspect CATE scores and subgroup estimates

The fitted object contains scores, available score coefficients, and estimated treatment effects in score-defined subgroups. These are results from the fitting sample, not an assessment of performance in new patients.

The fitted scores estimate conditional log rate ratios. The relationship
between covariates and the score depends on the scoring method. Here, lower
scores indicate greater estimated benefit from drug 1 because fewer relapses
are desirable. Pass `fit_cate` to `predict()` and choose a score with `method`:
`"poisson"`, `"boosting"`, or `"negative_binomial"` for the T-learners,
and `"two_regression"` or `"contrast_regression"` for the doubly robust
procedures. The returned scores correspond to the original analysis sample;
prediction for new data is not currently supported. Below are the first six
contrast-regression scores.

```{r print_catefit.score, eval = T, echo = T}
scores <- predict(fit_cate, method = "contrast_regression")
head(scores)
```

Use `plot()` to compare the fitted score distributions across methods. Scores
are on the log rate-ratio scale, with zero indicating a rate ratio of 1.

```{r plot_score, eval = T, echo = T, fig.align='center'}
plot(fit_cate, type = "density")
```

Differences in the score distributions can reflect model flexibility,
estimation noise or overfitting. The plot alone cannot distinguish these
explanations. Internal validation assesses whether the scores distinguish
subgroups in patients not used to fit them. Chapter 20 discusses score
distributions alongside validation curves [@jiang2026visualization].

Use `coef()` to extract available score coefficients and `confint()` to obtain
confidence intervals for contrast-regression coefficients. Boosting scores do
not have linear coefficients. The coefficients describe the fitted log
rate-ratio score and are not themselves a validation of that score.

```{r print_catefit.coefs, eval = T, echo = T}
coef(fit_cate, method = "contrast_regression")
confint(fit_cate, method = "contrast_regression")
```

Use `subgroup_estimates()` to inspect estimated rate ratios for nested
subgroups ranked by the contrast-regression score. These estimates use the same
data as the score fit; the validation section below assesses the score in
held-out data.

```{r print_catefit.ate, eval = T, echo = T}
subgroup_estimates(fit_cate, method = "contrast_regression", measure = "rate_ratio")
```

## Internally validate CATE scores

### How internal validation works

For broader guidance on validation strategies and the assessment of discrimination, calibration, and decision accuracy, see Chapter 19, "Validation of prediction models for patient outcomes and individualized treatment effect" [@thao2026validation].

In each iteration, the models are fitted in a training set and their scores are evaluated in a separate validation set. For example, the 50% of validation patients with the lowest predicted scores form a high-responder subgroup, and its estimated treatment effect can be compared with the overall effect. Repeating the split shows how results vary across iterations. Selecting the best method using these same validation results can make its reported performance optimistic; an independent evaluation is useful for assessing the selected method.

The `catecv()` function provides the same estimation as the `catefit()` but via cross-validation (CV). With the `catecv()` function internal CV is applied to reduce optimism in choosing the CATE estimation method that captures the most treatment effect heterogeneity. The CV is applied by repeating the following steps `cv.n` times:

* Split the data into a training and validation set according to `train.prop` argument. The training and validation sets must be balanced with respect to covariate distributions and doubly robust rate ratio estimates (see `error.max` argument).

* Estimate the CATE score in the training set with the specified scoring method.

* Predict the CATE score in the validation set using the scoring model fitted from the training set.

* Build nested subgroups of treatment responders in the training and validation sets, separately, and estimate the ATE within each nested subgroup. For each element i of `prop.cutoff` argument (e.g., `prop.cutoff[i] = 0.6`), take the following steps:

    * Identify high responders as observations with the 60% (i.e., `prop.cutoff[i]x100%`) highest (if `higher.y = TRUE`) or lowest (if `higher.y = FALSE`) estimated CATE scores.

    * Estimate the ATE in the subgroup of high responders using a doubly robust estimator.

    * Conversely, identify low responders as observations with the 40% (i.e., `1 - prop.cutoff[i]x100%`) lowest (if `higher.y = TRUE`) or highest (if `higher.y = FALSE`) estimated CATE scores.

    * Estimate the ATE in the subgroup of low responders using a doubly robust estimator.

* If `abc = TRUE`, calculate the area between the ATE and the series of ATEs in nested subgroups of high responders in the validation set. (for more information about the abc score, see [Validation curves and the ABC statistics](Theoretical-details.html))

* Build mutually exclusive subgroups of treatment responders in the training and validation sets, separately, and estimate the ATE within each subgroup. Mutually exclusive subgroups are built by splitting the estimated CATE scores according to prop.multi.


### Run internal validation

Now we can use the `catecv()` function to run internal validation to compare the different scoring methods. The mandatory arguments are similar to `atefit()` and `catefit()`: 
The mandatory arguments are: `response`, `data`, `score.method`, `cate.model`, and `ps.model`. For this toy example we selected `poisson`, `contrastReg` and `negBin` to limit run time. 

We also specified the following non-mandatory arguments to fit with the data and problem at hand: `initial.predictor.method`, `higher.y`, `cv.n` and `seed`.

* `initial.predictor.method` specifies how predictions of the outcome are estimated in two regressions and contrast regression. Flexible models can be used such as GBM ("boosting") or generalized additive models ("gam"). Both methods are computationally intensive so we choose "poisson" to obtain predictions from a Poisson regression, which reduces the computational time at the expense of stricter parametric assumptions and less flexibility.

For `twoReg` and `contrastReg`, the initial outcome models use the covariates in `cate.model` by default. To use additional outcome predictors while keeping a simpler CATE score, specify, for example, `init.model = y ~ age + female + previous_treatment + previous_cost`. The outcome must match `cate.model`; the exposure offset is taken from `cate.model`.

* `higher.y` was set to FALSE because lower number of relapses are more desirable in our example. Hence, we are telling the function that subgroups of high responders to drug1 vs drug0 should have lower number of relapses  (see section [Validation curves and the ABC statistics](Theoretical-details.html) for illustration). In other situation, higher outcomes may be more favorable, for example, walking more steps in a study on physical activity. It is important for this argument to match with the `y` outcome because it will affect how the subgroups are defined by the CATE scores and the performance metrics. 

* We perform 5 CV iterations by specifying `cv.n` = 5. Typically, more CV iterations are desirable although associated with longer computational times.

* We set a random seed `seed` = 999 to reproduce the results.

* Boosting performance plots are hidden by default; set `plot.gbmperf = TRUE` to display them.

There are many other non-mandatory arguments that `catecv()` can accept. Please see the [Customizing CATE models and validation](Additional-examples.html) vignette for more examples and the [Function description](https://smartdata-analysis-and-statistics.github.io/precmed/reference/catecvcount.html) section for details. If you run into errors or warnings with your data, it might be helpful to go over the descriptions to see if you need to alter the default values. In this toy example, we keep the default values of the remaining arguments.

```{r example_catecv, eval = T, echo = T, cache = doc.cache}
fit_cv <- catecv(
  response = "count",
  data = countExample,
  score.method = c("poisson", "contrastReg", "negBin"),
  cate.model = y ~ age + female + previous_treatment +
    previous_cost + previous_number_relapses + offset(log(years)),
  ps.model = trt ~ age + previous_treatment, 
  initial.predictor.method = "poisson",
  higher.y = FALSE,
  cv.n = 5, 
  seed = 999
)
```


### Inspect validation results

The output of `catecv()` is an object of class "precmed" and here we named it `fit_cv`. It carries the relevant information to use in the next step of the workflow which selects the method (among those specified in the argument `score.method`) capturing the highest level of treatment effect heterogeneity. The output, which is described below, will be used in the functions `abc()`, `plot()` and `boxplot()`.

For each method specified in the argument `score.method`, the following 3 groups of outputs are generated: `high`, `low` and `group`. We use the results from `contrastReg` as an example.

#### Nested subgroups of high responders

This output stores the ATEs - the ratio of annualized relapse rate between drug1 vs drug0 in this example - in nested subgroups of patients of high responders to drug 1 in the training (`$ate.est.train.high.cv`) and validation (`$ate.est.valid.high.cv`) sets across all CV iterations. For count outcomes, when `higher.y` = TRUE, higher CATE scores correspond to high responders to drug1. When `higher.y` = FALSE, lower CATE scores correspond to high responders to drug1. Note that this is different for survival outcomes. The direction of CATE scores depends on both `higher.y` and outcome type. 

```{r example_print_catecv, eval = T, echo = T}
fit_cv$ate.contrastReg$ate.est.train.high.cv
fit_cv$ate.contrastReg$ate.est.valid.high.cv
```

The output is a matrix with columns corresponding to the CV iterations, labeled from 1 to `cv.n`, and rows corresponding to nested subgroups. The nested subgroups of patients are defined by the argument `prop.cutoff`. Here, we use the default `seq(0.5, 1, length = 6)` which defines 6 nested subgroups with the 50\%, 60\%, 70\%, 80\%, 90\% and 100\% lowest (highest if `higher.y` = TRUE) CATE scores estimated by contrast regression. The rows in the output are labeled to reflect the user-specified proportions used to build the subgroups.

For example, in the training set and in the first CV iterations (first column labeled "cv1"), the subgroup defined with the 50\% lowest CATE scores (first row labeled "prop0.5") has an estimated RR of `r round(fit_cv$ate.contrastReg$ate.est.train.high.cv[1,1], 3)`. In contrast, the subgroup defined with all patients (last row labeled "prop1") has an estimated RR of `r round(fit_cv$ate.contrastReg$ate.est.train.high.cv[6,1], 3)`.
<!-- This suggests that the CATE score estimated with contrast regression identifies high responders to drug 1 vs drug 0 because patients with the 50\% lowest estimated CATE score have a better (lower) RR compared to all patients. However, the same relationship between estimated RRs is not observed in the training set. This will be further visualized with valiation curves in the next section. 
If higher outcomes were preferable (as specified through the argument `higher.y`), subgroups would be defined with proportion of patients with *highest* estimated CATE score and *higher* RR would be better. -->

#### Nested subgroups of low responders

This output stores the ATEs in nested subgroups of *low responders* to drug1 in the training (`$ate.est.train.low.cv`) and validation (`$ate.est.valid.low.cv`) sets across all CV iterations. For count outcomes, when `higher.y` = TRUE, lower CATE scores correspond to low responders to drug1. When `higher.y` = FALSE, higher CATE scores correspond to low responders to drug1. Again, this is different for survival outcomes. The direction of CATE scores depends on both `higher.y` and outcome type. 

```{r example_print_train_catecv, eval = T, echo = T}
fit_cv$ate.contrastReg$ate.est.train.low.cv
```
The outputs are also matrices with columns corresponding to the CV iterations and rows corresponding to nested subgroups. 

The output for the low responders brings additional information to the user. It gives the ATEs in the complement of each nested subgroup of high responders. For example, the complement of the subgroup of high responders defined as patients with the 60\% lowest (highest if `higher.y` = TRUE) estimated CATE scores is the subgroup low responders defined as patients with the 40\% highest (lowest if `higher.y` = TRUE) estimated CATE scores, labeled as "prop0.4". In the training set and in the first CV iterations, the estimated RR is `r round(fit_cv$ate.contrastReg$ate.est.train.high.cv[2,1], 3)` in the 60\% high responders to drug 1 and `r round(fit_cv$ate.contrastReg$ate.est.train.low.cv[2,1], 3)` in the 40\% low responders.

#### Mutually exclusive subgroups

This output stores the ATEs in mutually exclusive multi-category subgroups of patients in the training (`$ate.est.train.group.cv`) and validation (`$ate.est.valid.group.cv`) sets across all CV iterations. 

```{r example_print_group_catecv, eval = T, echo = T}
fit_cv$ate.contrastReg$ate.est.train.group.cv
fit_cv$ate.contrastReg$ate.est.valid.group.cv
```

The output is a matrix with columns corresponding to the CV iterations and rows corresponding to the mutually exclusive subgroups. The previous 2 outputs only focus on binary subgroups (high or low responders). Here, the mutually exclusive subgroups can be more than 2 and are defined by the argument `prop.multi`. We use the default `c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1)` which defines 3 subgroups of patients with the 33\% lowest, 33\% middle and 33\% highest estimated CATE scores when `higher.y` = FALSE (as in this example), or with the 33\% highest, 33\% middle and 33\% lowest estimated CATE scores when `higher.y` = TRUE. Taking the first column as an example, the first CV iteration calculated `r round(fit_cv$ate.contrastReg$ate.est.train.group.cv[1,1], 3)` as the RR for the subgroup with the 33\% lowest estimated CATE scores, `r round(fit_cv$ate.contrastReg$ate.est.train.group.cv[2,1], 3)` as the RR for subgroup with the 33\% middle estimated CATE scores, and `r round(fit_cv$ate.contrastReg$ate.est.train.group.cv[3,1], 3)` as the RR for subgroup with the 33\% highest estimated CATE scores.


### Inspect errors and warnings

Subgroup estimates can be missing or unstable, for example when a subgroup has few patients or observed events. Tied scores can also leave a subgroup empty or change its size from the requested proportion. Use `diagnostics()` to inspect recorded subgroup errors, warnings, unavailable ABC values and contrast-regression convergence across methods, splits and iterations. An empty table means no such messages were recorded; it does not establish that the models fit well.

```{r errwarn, eval = T, echo = T}
diagnostics(fit_cv)
```

The support table records the number of patients (`n0`, `n1`) and total observed relapses (`events0`, `events1`) in each treatment arm for each reported subgroup. For example, inspect the first six validation-set support records for contrast regression with:

```{r count_support, eval = T, echo = T}
head(subset(fit_cv$subgroup.support,
            split == "validation" & method == "contrastReg",
            select = c(iteration, group, subgroup, n0, n1, events0, events1)))
```

The contrast-regression convergence vector indicates whether at least one cross-fitting repetition converged in each CV iteration. The individual repetition results are available in `fit_cv$ate.contrastReg$converge.repetitions.cv`.

## Compare scoring methods using the ABC statistic

The ABC statistics is calculated by `abc()` for each scoring method specified in `catecv()` and for each of the `cv.n` CV iterations using the output object `fit_cv` from `catecv()`.

Each validation curve summarizes estimated treatment effects in nested high-responder groups, from a smaller group with more favorable scores to the entire validation set. The ABC summarizes the area between that curve and the overall ATE reference line; a higher value indicates greater separation in the expected direction for this example. Chapter 20 describes this responder diagnostic and its interpretation [@jiang2026visualization]. See the [Validation curves and the ABC statistics](Theoretical-details.html) section for a detailed illustration of the relationship between `higher.y`, `abc`, and the validation curves. 

```{r example_abc, eval = T, echo = T}
abc(fit_cv)
```

The output is a matrix with columns corresponding to the CV iterations and rows corresponding to the scoring methods specified in `score.method`. Individual iterations can differ; summarize across iterations to compare methods:

```{r example_abc_combine, eval = T, echo = T}
abc(fit_cv, combine = "mean")
```

In this example, negative binomial also offers the best overall performance because it has the highest average ABC, followed closely by Poisson.

## Assess responder discrimination with validation curves

Chapter 20 discusses validation curves, ABC statistics, and their interpretation as responder diagnostics [@jiang2026visualization]. These summaries assess how well a score ranks patients by treatment benefit; they do not, by themselves, establish calibration of the predicted CATEs or the clinical value of a treatment rule [@thao2026validation].

The ATEs of nested subgroups of high responders to drug1 (e.g., `fit_cv$ate.contrastReg$ate.est.train.high.cv` and `fit_cv$ate.contrastReg$ate.est.valid.high.cv` for contrast regression) can be visualized as a side-by-side line plot, with training results on the left and validation results on the right. The x-axis is determined by `prop.cutoff` and the y-axis is the estimated ATEs averaged over `cv.n` CV iterations as specified by `cv.i` = NULL. The estimated ATE is expressed as a RR of drug1 versus drug0 for our toy example. By default, the function retrieves the name of the treatment variable (`trt`) and the original labels (`drug0` and `drug1`) to specify a meaningful y-axis label.

Steeper slopes indicate more treatment effect heterogeneity between drug1 and drug0. Because `higher.y` = FALSE in this example, the slopes should be increasing from left (`prop.cutoff` = 0.5) to right (`prop.cutoff` = 1) if treatment effect heterogeneity is present. The method that has the steepest slope in the validation results would be selected because it captures the most treatment effect heterogeneity while generalizing well to unseen data.


```{r example_plot_lineplot1, eval = T, echo = T}
plot(fit_cv)
```

For this toy example, the methods are performing well in the training data as per the steep, increasing slopes on the left plot. The generally increasing curves in the validation data (right plot) are consistent with the scores ranking patients by treatment benefit in this example, although they do not alone establish generalizability or calibration. The dashed gray line is the ATE in the entire data set, which is why all lines merge to this reference line when subgroup size is 100\% of the data (`prop.cutoff` = 1). For more explanation on the validation curves, see the [Function description](https://smartdata-analysis-and-statistics.github.io/precmed/reference/plot.precmed.html) section. 

The plot's legend includes the ABC statistics in the validation set. The user can choose to mute the ABC annotations by specifying `show.abc` = FALSE.

```{r example_plot_lineplot1.1, eval = T, echo = T}
plot(fit_cv, show.abc = FALSE)
```

To compare training and validation curves directly for each scoring method, use `layout = "method"`. Each panel shows one method, with a solid training curve and a dashed validation curve. The dotted lines mark the corresponding overall treatment effects.

```{r example_plot_by_method, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 7}
plot(fit_cv, layout = "method", show.abc = FALSE)
```

To plot validation curves for a single CV iteration instead of the average, specify `cv.i` (for example, `cv.i = 2` for the second iteration). Set `grayscale = TRUE` to display the curves in grayscale.

Same as `abc()`, the user can also choose to use the median (instead of mean [default]) of the ATEs across CV iterations by specifying the argument `combine` = "median" in `plot()`. 

## Compare treatment effects across responder subgroups

Unlike the nested groups in the validation curves, these groups are mutually exclusive: each patient belongs to one score-based group in a given validation iteration. Each box summarizes the variation in that group’s estimated treatment effect across iterations. Chapter 20 compares these complementary responder diagnostics [@jiang2026visualization]. 

The ATEs of multi-category subgroups that are mutually exclusive can be visualized as box plots, with one box plot for each scoring method. Only validation results are visualized here. The x-axis is determined by `prop.multi` and the y-axis is the estimated ATEs in each subgroup. The default y-axis label identifies the treatment contrast. The subgroups correspond to each row of the `ate.est.valid.group.cv` result in `fit_cv`, so in this example the subgroups are patient with the 33\% lowest (0-33\%), middle 33\% (33-66\%), and highest 33\% (66-100\%) estimated CATE scores. The box plot shows the distribution of the ATEs over all `cv.n` CV iterations, instead of a summary statistics like mean or median in `plot()`.

```{r example_plot_boxplot, eval = T, echo = T}
boxplot(fit_cv)
```

The box plots compare estimated rate ratios across mutually exclusive score-based subgroups. Read them alongside the validation curves and ABC statistics to assess how each scoring method separates patients by treatment benefit and how estimates vary across CV iterations. Note that the y-axis can have different scales for different scoring methods.

<br><br>

> Although we provided 3 different metrics to summarize and visualize the `catecv()` outputs, the user is encouraged to choose their own way of data wrangling that fits to their particular situation.
